rationale: All 6 candidates are direct matches by trait/efo and have endpoint-faithful phenotyping_reported (“Abdominal aortic aneurysm” or closely equivalent; one is explicitly prevalent). The strongest disease-focused evidence package appears to be the Nat Genet AAA GWAS meta-analysis family (PGS003972/PGS003973): multi-cohort disease study context with PRS-CS genome-wide modeling and European evaluation. Between the two, PGS003972 is favored because it reports a full-model AUROC (0.69) without the exceptionally high C-index seen in PGS003973 (0.882), which—given only basic covariates shown—may reflect non-comparable modeling/endpoint handling and is not accompanied by PRS-only metrics; avoiding reliance on a single outlier full-model discrimination aligns with the provided policy. Remaining limitation: across all candidates, PRS-only AUROC and incremental AUROC are largely missing, covariates are unknown for some (including PGS003972), and the available metrics are not directly comparable (partial-r, covariates-regressed-out R2, full-model AUROC/C-index), preventing a high-confidence ‘best’ selection.

All 6 candidates are direct matches by trait_reported/trait_efo and have endpoint-faithful phenotyping_reported (abdominal aortic aneurysm; one is explicitly prevalent AAA). PGS000753 comes from a disease-focused AAA study (MVP/Mayo-VDB; Circulation), reports a clear per-SD effect size (OR=1.37, 95% CI 1.30–1.44) with basic covariates (age, sex, PCs), and has moderate validation size (n=46,564). Competing candidates either come from framework/portability contexts with PRS-only metrics that are small and/or not cleanly comparable (PGS001784 has covariates-regressed-out R2=0.0147 but is from a global biobank framework and its AUROC=0.868 is a full-model metric with extensive covariates; PGS002054 is a UKB portability score with only partial-r=0.0144), or report only full-model AUROC/C-index with unknown covariates (PGS003429/PGS003972) or potentially covariate-driven discrimination (PGS003973 C-index=0.882 with only age/sex shown but no isolated PRS-only metric). Overall, the absence of consistently reported, directly comparable PRS-only AUC/R2 across the set—especially for the newer disease-focused PRS-CS models—prevents a high-confidence best-choice, so the selection remains sub-optimal despite a reasonable preference for PGS000753’s disease-focused context and interpretable effect-size evidence.

All 6 candidates are direct matches (trait_reported/trait_efo align to abdominal aortic aneurysm; phenotyping_reported is AAA in each, though one is explicitly prevalent). For selection, disease-family policy for cardiovascular/large-vessel traits prefers disease-focused multi-cohort meta-analysis models with exact endpoints and basic covariates over older prevalent-endpoint sparse models and over pan-trait/portability frameworks. PGS003972/PGS003973 come from a dedicated AAA GWAS meta-analysis (Nat Genet) using PRS-CS and many contributing cohorts, but their reported discrimination is only via full-model AUROC/C-index (not PGS-only) and covariates are unknown or minimal, making cross-model PRS comparability unclear; PGS003973’s high C-index (0.882) is therefore not interpretable as PRS contribution. PGS001784 (Global Biobank framework) and PGS002054 (UKB portability framework) are explicitly framework-style and should be down-ranked versus disease-focused studies absent clearly stronger PRS-comparable metrics. Given the limited availability of PRS-only discrimination metrics across candidates and the interpretability issues of full-model AUC/C-index, the best-supported choice from visible evidence is PGS000753, but with only moderate confidence.

All listed candidates are direct matches at the trait/efo level, but several have endpoint-fidelity issues for generic hypothyroidism deployment (e.g., therapy-induced hypothyroidism in cancer patients: PGS000759/PGS000761/PGS000820) or are pan-trait / portability framework scores (e.g., snpnet across 813 traits: PGS000965/PGS001181; UKB portability: PGS001816/PGS002024). PGS005218 is the most disease-focused and largest-scale hypothyroidism-specific model in the set (Nat Genet GWAS and PRS prediction of hypothyroidism; training n=1,146,562 across multiple cohorts; validation n=441,692; European evaluation) and reports strong discrimination (full-model AUROC=0.859). However, its covariates include thyroid biomarkers (TSH, T4, anti-TPO), which the provided domain knowledge flags as near-outcome covariates that can severely inflate full-model AUROC; no PRS-only or incremental metrics are shown here to isolate the PRS contribution. This makes the evidence insufficient to call a clearly high-quality standalone PRS winner despite the otherwise strong study/validation support.

Multiple direct-match models are present for hypothyroidism, but the strongest-looking recent model (PGS005218) reports a very high full-model AUROC (0.859) while explicitly including thyroid biomarkers (TSH, T4, anti-TPO) as covariates, which the provided domain guidance flags as near-outcome covariates that can severely inflate/obscure PRS contribution; no PRS-only AUROC/R2 is shown for that model here, so its performance is not comparable. Among candidates with cleaner/less clearly inflating covariates and explicit discrimination, PGS004935 (Hypothyroidism; SnpNet; UKB-trained; EUR eval) reports AUROC=0.70 and OR=1.5 (1.41–1.6) with a defined validation sample (n=8,417), whereas several other non-treatment endpoints either lack AUROC/R2 entirely (e.g., PGS002766, PGS001816/PGS002024) or are from therapy-induced hypothyroidism endpoints (PGS000759/PGS000761/PGS000820) that are less endpoint-faithful for generic hypothyroidism. All five candidates are direct matches on `trait_reported`/`trait_efo` to late-onset Alzheimer’s disease, but their endpoint and performance evidence are uneven. PGS000053 and PGS000054 come from the same disease-focused publication with a clear endpoint (`phenotyping_reported`: familial late-onset Alzheimer’s disease) and provide interpretable PRS effect-size evidence (per-SD OR). Between them, PGS000054 has the strongest reported effect size (OR=1.73, 95% CI 1.57–1.93) and does not rely on heavy covariates (only age, sex), making it the best-supported signal of PRS discrimination among the set. Key limitations: (1) no PRS-comparable AUROC/R² is reported for these models; (2) PGS000054’s evaluation ancestry is AMR-only, so without a specified intended deployment ancestry its transportability relative to the EUR-evaluated alternative (PGS000053) is uncertain; (3) competing models either have potentially non-comparable or concerning metrics (e.g., PGS000334 reports R²=0.191 from C+T with unknown covariates, which the provided domain guidance flags as potentially inflated/non-comparable) or phenotype misalignment/noisy phenotyping (PGS002289’s `phenotyping_reported` is cognition-by-age interaction rather than a direct LOAD diagnosis), or very small validation (PGS004918 n=136 with only full-model AUROC). These gaps prevent a high-confidence ‘best’ choice despite preferring PGS000054 on effect-size and clean covariate disclosure.

All 5 candidates are direct matches at the trait/EFO level (late-onset Alzheimer’s disease), but endpoint fidelity and performance reporting are uneven. PGS000053 and PGS000054 come from the same disease-focused publication and have clear late-onset AD phenotyping (“Familial late-onset Alzheimer’s disease (LOAD)”) plus basic covariates (age, sex) and interpretable per-SD effect sizes; among them, PGS000054 shows a materially stronger reported OR (1.73, 95% CI 1.57–1.93) than PGS000053 (OR 1.29), which the domain policy suggests can break ties within a study family. Other candidates have key limitations: PGS000334 reports a high R²=0.191 under C+T with unknown covariates, which domain guidance flags as potentially inflated/non-comparable for a complex trait; PGS004918 reports only a full-model AUROC=0.731 with unknown covariates and very small validation (n=136), and the policy cautions against treating full-model AUROC as PRS-comparable; PGS002289’s phenotyping_reported appears misaligned (cognition × age interaction rather than AD diagnosis), despite the trait label. Overall, a direct-match candidate is present and PGS000054 is best-supported by coherent endpoint + clean covariates + strongest effect size, but the absence of PRS-comparable AUC/R² across the leading family and uncertainty about deployment ancestry (EUR vs AMR evaluation) keep this at sub-optimal rather than high-quality.

All five candidates are direct matches on trait_reported/trait_efo, but endpoint fidelity differs. PGS002289 is down-ranked because its phenotyping_reported is a cognition×age interaction rather than a direct LOAD diagnosis endpoint, despite the large validation sample. PGS000053/PGS000054 and PGS000334/PGS004918 have diagnosis-anchored phenotyping_reported (familial LOAD or LOAD) and disease-focused publication contexts, making them better endpoint matches. Among the diagnosis-anchored models, performance reporting is limited/inconsistent: PGS000053/PGS000054 provide per-SD ORs (1.29 EUR; 1.73 Hispanic/Latin American) but no AUC/R2; PGS000334 reports R²=0.191 from a C+T score with unknown covariates, which is unusually high relative to the local heritability sanity-check (h2_obs=0.0084; h2_liability=0.0269) and therefore may be inflated or non-comparable; PGS004918 reports only a full-model AUROC=0.731 with very small validation n=136 and unknown covariates, and domain guidance cautions against treating full-model AUROC as PRS-comparable. Given domain policy for late-onset neurodegenerative diseases (familial late-onset forms remain direct matches) and that stronger effect sizes can outweigh modest validation differences within a study family, PGS000054 is preferred over PGS000053 because it shows a materially stronger per-SD OR (1.73 vs 1.29) while sharing the same study family and sparse-SNP construction. Confidence is moderated because the candidates use different evaluation ancestries (EUR vs AMR) and lack directly comparable PRS-only AUC/R2 metrics across models.
